## Summary

Implement the shared test infrastructure in `internal/common/testutil/` that all operator integration and E2E tests will depend on. This includes: an envtest bootstrap function starting a local API server + etcd with project and external CRDs; minimal fake CRD YAML schemas for five external operators (MariaDB, ESO, cert-manager, Memcached, RabbitMQ); a `SecretBuilder` establishing the fluent builder pattern; external operator simulators that patch CR status to mimic readiness; custom gomega assertion helpers for condition checking and resource existence; and a Chainsaw E2E directory structure with global configuration targeting Chainsaw v0.3+.

## Scope

**Included:**
- `internal/common/testutil/envtest/` — `SetupEnvTest()` function: starts `envtest.Environment`, installs CRDs from `config/crd/bases` (own) and `fake_crds/` (external), registers schemes, returns `*rest.Config` + `client.Client` + teardown func. Follows the pattern from `architecture/06-testing.md:90-104`
- `internal/common/testutil/fake_crds/` — Minimal CRD YAML schemas (only fields operators interact with: `.status.conditions`, `.status.ready`, referenced `.spec` fields) for: MariaDB Operator (`MariaDB`, `Database`, `User`, `Grant`), ESO (`ExternalSecret`, `PushSecret`, `ClusterSecretStore`), cert-manager (`Certificate`, `ClusterIssuer`), Memcached Operator (`Memcached`), RabbitMQ Cluster Operator (`RabbitmqCluster`)
- `internal/common/testutil/builders/` — `SecretBuilder` with chainable `WithName()`, `WithNamespace()`, `WithData()`, `WithStringData()`, `WithLabels()`, `WithOwnerRef()`, `Build()`, `Create(ctx, client)`. Establishes the fluent builder pattern that operator-specific builders (S011/S019) will follow
- `internal/common/testutil/simulators/` — `SimulateMariaDBReady(ctx, client, name, namespace)`, `SimulateMemcachedReady(...)`, `SimulateExternalSecretSync(...)`, `SimulateJobComplete(...)` — each creates the CR if absent, then patches its status to indicate readiness
- `internal/common/testutil/assertions/` — `AssertCondition(g, conditions, condType, status)`, `EventuallyCondition(ctx, client, obj, condType, status, timeout)`, `AssertResourceExists(ctx, client, key, obj)`, `AssertResourceNotExists(ctx, client, key, obj)`
- `tests/e2e/chainsaw-config.yaml` — Global Chainsaw v0.3+ configuration (`apiVersion: chainsaw.kyverno.io/v1alpha1`, default timeouts, cleanup, parallel, JUnit output)
- `tests/e2e/{keystone,c5c3,infrastructure}/.gitkeep` — Directory placeholders
- Unit tests for assertions and builders; integration test verifying `SetupEnvTest()` starts/stops cleanly

**Excluded (with rationale):**
- `KeystoneBuilder`, `ControlPlaneBuilder` — API types don't exist until S011/S019; builder pattern established via `SecretBuilder` (YAGNI)
- Actual Chainsaw test scenarios — S012, S016, S022; only directory structure and config here
- CI pipeline integration — S003
- Makefile `test-integration` / `install-test-deps` targets — S001 stubs, S003 implements
- Controller-runtime reconciler test wiring — S014, reconciler-specific
- OpenBao/ESO test doubles beyond `SimulateExternalSecretSync` — S010

## Key Components

- **`testutil/envtest/setup.go`** — `SetupEnvTest(crdPaths ...string) (*rest.Config, client.Client, func())`: boots envtest with API server + etcd, installs CRDs from provided paths plus `fake_crds/`, registers all relevant schemes (core, apps, batch + external operator types), returns config + client + teardown closure
- **`testutil/fake_crds/{mariadb,eso,cert-manager,memcached,rabbitmq}/`** — Minimal CRD YAMLs defining only the spec/status fields operators interact with. Derived from `internal/common/database/`, `secrets/`, `tls/` function signatures in `architecture/02-shared-library.md`
- **`testutil/builders/secret.go`** — Fluent `SecretBuilder` returning `*corev1.Secret`. Pattern reference for operator-specific builders added in S011/S019
- **`testutil/simulators/{mariadb,memcached,externalsecret,job}.go`** — Create external CRs with ready status to simulate third-party operator behavior in envtest. Each creates the CR if absent, patches `.status.ready = true` and condition `Ready=True`
- **`testutil/assertions/conditions.go`** — Typed gomega helpers: `EventuallyCondition` polls via `Eventually()` + `client.Get()` until condition reaches expected status
- **`testutil/assertions/resources.go`** — `AssertResourceExists` / `AssertResourceNotExists` for existence checks
- **`tests/e2e/chainsaw-config.yaml`** — Global Chainsaw v0.3+ config: 120s assert timeout, 30s apply timeout, cleanup enabled, parallel execution, JUnit report output
- **`tests/e2e/{keystone,c5c3,infrastructure}/.gitkeep`** — Empty directory structure for future test scenarios

**User Stories:**
- **developer** wants to call a single SetupEnvTest() function that starts a local API server + etcd with all project and external CRDs installed so that I can write integration tests against a real Kubernetes API without deploying a full cluster
- **developer** wants minimal CRD YAML schemas for MariaDB, ESO, cert-manager, Memcached, and RabbitMQ operators that define only the fields our code interacts with so that integration tests can create, read, and patch external operator CRs without installing the full operator CRDs
- **developer** wants a chainable builder for Kubernetes Secrets with WithName(), WithNamespace(), WithData(), WithStringData(), WithLabels(), WithOwnerRef(), Build(), and Create() so that I can construct test Secrets concisely and consistently, establishing the builder pattern for future operator-specific builders
- **developer** wants simulator functions that create external CRs if absent and patch their status to indicate readiness so that integration tests can test reconciler logic that depends on external operators being ready without running those operators
- **developer** wants typed gomega helpers for checking metav1.Condition status and Kubernetes resource existence so that integration tests can assert condition state and resource lifecycle with readable, reusable assertions
- **developer** wants a global Chainsaw v0.3+ configuration and placeholder directories for keystone, c5c3, and infrastructure E2E tests so that future E2E test tasks (S012, S016, S022) can add test scenarios without setting up the Chainsaw config from scratch
- **developer** wants unit tests for builders and assertions, and an integration test proving SetupEnvTest starts and stops cleanly so that the shared test infrastructure is validated before downstream features depend on it
- **developer** wants a reference doc describing all testutil packages, their functions, signatures, and usage examples so that I can use the shared test infrastructure without reading all source files

    <requirement>Search codebase for existing patterns before creating new</requirement>
    <violation>Redundant implementations rejected</violation>
  </rule>
  <rule id="6" name="NO_SCOPE_CREEP">
    <requirement>Implement only what is explicitly requested</requirement>
    <violation>Extra features removed, effort wasted</violation>
  </rule>
  <rule id="7" name="TYPE_SAFE">
    <requirement>All code must pass mypy (Python), tsc (TypeScript), or go vet (Go) strict checks</requirement>
    <violation>Type errors block merge - no type: ignore without justification</violation>
  </rule>
  <rule id="8" name="LINT_CLEAN">
    <requirement>All code must pass ruff (Python), eslint (TypeScript), or golangci-lint (Go) without errors</requirement>
    <violation>Lint errors block merge - run ruff check/eslint/golangci-lint before completion</violation>
  </rule>
  <rule id="9" name="TEST_COVERAGE">
    <requirement>New/modified code must have accompanying tests - no untested code</requirement>
    <violation>Untested code rejected in review - write tests FIRST (TDD)</violation>
  </rule>
  <rule id="10" name="NO_BASH_TASKS">
    <requirement>Use native TaskCreate/TaskList/TaskUpdate for task management — never Bash scripts or filesystem workarounds</requirement>
    <violation>Bash-based task creation is fragile and breaks tracking</violation>
  </rule>
  <rule id="11" name="FEATURE_ID_REQUIRED">
    <requirement>When referencing requirements, tests, tasks, or user stories in docs, docstrings, comments, or commit messages — ALWAYS include the Feature ID</requirement>
    <examples>
      <bad>"Fixes the login bug", "See related task", "As per requirement"</bad>
      <good>"Fixes login bug (F-0042)", "See task F-0042", "As per requirement F-0042"</good>
    </examples>
    <violation>References without Feature ID are untraceable and rejected in review</violation>
  </rule>
</critical-rules>


<review-process>
  <step order="1">Run `git diff` or `git status` to see modified files</step>
  <step order="2">Verify tests exist and pass</step>
  <step order="3">Check against review criteria above</step>
  <step order="4">Security review (OWASP Top 10, input validation)</step>
  <step order="5">Document ALL findings in JSON</step>
</review-process>


<review-pattern-scan>
<purpose>
  Systematic detection of codebase patterns to enforce consistency.
  This is a DEDICATED review step — not optional.
  Goal: same problem, same approach, everywhere.

  QUALITY OVER QUANTITY: A small set of meaningful, well-established patterns
  is infinitely more valuable than a large set of trivially observed ones.
  Every persisted pattern creates enforcement cost in future reviews.
  Only persist a pattern when it genuinely prevents inconsistency at scale —
  not because you noticed a coding choice that could theoretically recur.
</purpose>

<scan-process>
  <step order="1" name="INVENTORY">
    For EVERY changed file, list the structural patterns used:
    - Error handling approach (custom exceptions? error codes? Result type?)
    - Service/module structure (class-based? function-based?)
    - Dependency injection (constructor injection? global registry? provider pattern?)
    - Data access approach (repository classes? direct queries? ORM? raw SQL?)
    - API design (endpoint structure? schema definition? response envelope?)
    - Naming conventions (prefixes, suffixes, casing beyond PEP 8)
    - Test organization (fixture usage, test naming, arrangement pattern)
    - Import style (relative? absolute? lazy? conditional?)
    - Configuration access (env vars? settings object? constants?)
    - Logging approach (structured? unstructured? log levels?)
    - Validation approach (Pydantic? manual? decorators?)
  </step>

  <step order="2" name="COMPARE">
    For each pattern found in step 1, search the existing codebase:
    - Is this pattern already used elsewhere? How?
    - Are there DIFFERENT approaches for the SAME concern?
    - Example: File A uses `raise CustomError(...)` but File B uses `return None`
      for the same kind of failure — this is an INCONSISTENCY.
  </step>

  <step order="3" name="DETECT-INCONSISTENCIES">
    Flag every case where:
    - Two files solve the same problem differently
    - A new file introduces a novel approach when an established one exists
    - An existing pattern was partially followed (some parts match, some diverge)
    - A pattern from .planwerk/patterns/ was ignored or modified
    Mark these as severity=BLOCKING with check-id PC3.
  </step>

  <step order="4" name="IDENTIFY-NEW-PATTERNS">
    ONLY identify a new pattern if ALL of the following are true:
    - It is STRUCTURAL (affects how code is organized/composed), not a trivial style choice
    - It is ALREADY used in 2+ places in the codebase, OR it is a deliberate architectural
      decision that WILL recur (e.g. a new base class, a shared utility convention)
    - Persisting it would PREVENT a realistic inconsistency risk — ask: "If another
      developer touches a similar file next week, would they plausibly do it differently
      without this pattern documented?" If no, don't persist it.
    - It is NOT already covered by an existing pattern in .planwerk/patterns/
      (check for overlap by category+component before emitting)

    If the above threshold is met, document it:
    - What is the pattern? (concrete description, not vague)
    - Which component/layer does it apply to?
    - When should it be applied? (specific trigger condition)
    - Include 1-2 COMPLETE code samples from the actual source files
    - Each sample must include the file:line location AND the full code snippet
      (code changes over time and line numbers shift — the embedded code preserves
      the snapshot so future readers can understand the pattern even if the file changed)

    When in doubt, do NOT emit a pattern. A missed pattern can be added later;
    a noise pattern pollutes every future review.
  </step>

  <step order="5" name="VERIFY-CODEBASE-COVERAGE">
    For EVERY new pattern identified in step 4:
    - Search the ENTIRE codebase for locations where this pattern should apply
    - Produce a coverage report: where applied, where missing
    - If the pattern is only partially applied (some locations follow it, others don't):
      mark as severity=BLOCKING with check-id NPC1
    - The pattern must be applied EVERYWHERE it is relevant — no partial adoption
  </step>

  <step order="6" name="OUTPUT">
    Add detected patterns to the review JSON in the detected_patterns array.
    Each entry must have: name, component, category, applies_when, description, examples.
    Each example is an object with "location" (file_path:line_number) and "code"
    (the actual code snippet — include enough lines to show the full pattern,
    typically 5-20 lines).

    HARD REQUIREMENT: Only include patterns that are CONFIRMED — used in 2+ places
    in the actual codebase. A single occurrence is a coding choice, not a pattern.
    The one exception: an explicit architectural decision (new base class, shared
    convention) where the INTENT to reuse is obvious from the code itself (e.g. an
    abstract base class, a factory, a shared decorator). Even then, apply the
    threshold from step 4 strictly.

    FINAL CHECK before emitting detected_patterns: review the list and remove any
    entry that a developer would look at and think "why is this a pattern?". If the
    answer isn't immediately obvious, drop it.
  </step>
</scan-process>

<categories>
  <category name="error-handling">How errors are created, raised, caught, reported</category>
  <category name="service-structure">How services/modules are organized and composed</category>
  <category name="data-access">How data is read, written, queried, cached</category>
  <category name="validation">How input is validated and sanitized</category>
  <category name="testing">How tests are structured, fixtures used, assertions made</category>
  <category name="configuration">How config values are loaded and accessed</category>
  <category name="naming">Naming conventions beyond language defaults</category>
  <category name="api-design">How endpoints, schemas, responses are structured</category>
  <category name="logging">How logging, metrics, observability are handled</category>
  <category name="dependency-injection">How dependencies are provided and wired</category>
  <category name="import-style">How modules are imported: relative vs absolute, lazy vs eager, conditional</category>
</categories>

<consistency-rules>
  <rule priority="1">If a mandatory pattern exists in .planwerk/patterns/, it MUST be used — no exceptions</rule>
  <rule priority="2">If 3+ files use the same approach, that IS the pattern — new code must follow it</rule>
  <rule priority="3">If 2 different approaches exist for the same concern, flag as inconsistency and recommend which one to standardize on</rule>
  <rule priority="4">When introducing a genuinely new pattern, it must be documented in detected_patterns</rule>
  <rule priority="5">A new pattern MUST be applied to ALL matching locations in the codebase — partial adoption is BLOCKING (NPC1)</rule>
</consistency-rules>

<anti-patterns>
  <example type="bad" label="Missed inconsistency">
    Reviewer says "APPROVED" but file_a.py uses dataclasses while file_b.py uses
    TypedDict for the same kind of DTO — both in the same module.
  </example>
  <example type="good" label="Caught inconsistency">
    PC3: models/user.py uses @dataclass for DTOs (line 15-30) but models/order.py
    uses TypedDict (line 8-20) for the same purpose. Standardize on @dataclass
    per existing pattern in models/. Fix: convert order.py TypedDict to @dataclass.
  </example>
  <example type="bad" label="Vague pattern">
    detected_patterns: [{"name": "Good error handling", ...}]
    Problem: "Good" is not a pattern description.
  </example>
  <example type="bad" label="Pattern proliferation — trivial observation persisted">
    detected_patterns: [{"name": "Type hints on functions", "applies_when": "Writing functions",
    "description": "All functions have type hints."}]
    Problem: This is a language-level convention (enforced by mypy), NOT a codebase pattern.
    Do not persist things that are already enforced by linters, formatters, or language rules.
  </example>
  <example type="bad" label="Pattern proliferation — single occurrence persisted">
    detected_patterns: [{"name": "Retry decorator on API calls", ...}]
    but only ONE function in the entire codebase uses this decorator.
    Problem: One occurrence is a coding choice, not a pattern. Wait until it recurs.
  </example>
  <example type="good" label="Concrete pattern with code samples">
    detected_patterns: [{"name": "Custom exception hierarchy with domain prefix",
    "applies_when": "Creating new error types in any service module",
    "description": "All custom exceptions inherit from PlanwerkError. Named as
    {Domain}{Failure}Error (e.g. FeatureNotFoundError). Include context dict in __init__.",
    "examples": [
      {"location": "planwerk/errors.py:12",
       "code": "class FeatureNotFoundError(PlanwerkError):\n    def __init__(self, feature_id: str) -> None:\n        super().__init__(f\"Feature {feature_id} not found\", context={\"feature_id\": feature_id})"},
      {"location": "planwerk/services/storage.py:45",
       "code": "class StorageWriteError(PlanwerkError):\n    def __init__(self, path: str, reason: str) -> None:\n        super().__init__(f\"Failed to write {path}: {reason}\", context={\"path\": path})"}
    ]}]
  </example>

  <example type="bad" label="New pattern only partially applied">
    New pattern "structured logging with context dict" found in services/billing.py
    but services/auth.py and services/orders.py still use unstructured logging.
    Reviewer says APPROVED without checking full codebase coverage.
  </example>
  <example type="good" label="Full codebase coverage report for new pattern">
    NPC1: New pattern "structured logging with context dict" — Coverage report:
    Applied: services/billing.py:23, services/billing.py:45
    Missing: services/auth.py:12 (uses f-string logging), services/orders.py:34 (uses % formatting)
    Verdict: BLOCKING — pattern must be applied to all 4 locations.
  </example>
</anti-patterns>
</review-pattern-scan>

## Description

Every operator main.go follows an identical structure: package-level scheme var, init() with clientgoscheme.AddToScheme + kubebuilder scaffold:scheme marker, main() calling bootstrap.Run(bootstrap.ManagerConfig{...}) with operator-specific Scheme, LeaderElectionID, and SetupFunc. Error handling logs via ctrl.Log.WithName("setup").Error() then os.Exit(1). The bootstrap package centralises flag parsing, zap logging, metrics, health probes, and manager lifecycle — operators only provide configuration.

## Examples

### `operators/keystone/main.go:1-40`

```go
package main

import (
	"os"

	"github.com/c5c3/forge/internal/common/bootstrap"

	"k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime"
	utilruntime "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/runtime"
	clientgoscheme "k8s.io/client-go/kubernetes/scheme"
	ctrl "sigs.k8s.io/controller-runtime"
)

var scheme = runtime.NewScheme()

func init() {
	utilruntime.Must(clientgoscheme.AddToScheme(scheme))
	// +kubebuilder:scaffold:scheme
}

func main() {
	if err := bootstrap.Run(bootstrap.ManagerConfig{
		Scheme:           scheme,
		LeaderElectionID: "keystone.openstack.c5c3.io",
		SetupFunc: func(_ ctrl.Manager) error {
			// +kubebuilder:scaffold:builder — register controllers here
			return nil
		},
	}); err != nil {
		ctrl.Log.WithName("setup").Error(err, "unable to run manager")
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}
```

<review-guidelines>
<thinking required="before-review">
  <step order="1" name="INTENT">What was the task trying to achieve? Read the plan.</step>
  <step order="2" name="SCOPE">Did changes stay within requested scope? Any scope creep? Review scope = files in git diff ONLY — do not generate findings for unchanged files.</step>
  <step order="3" name="VERIFICATION">Run pytest, mypy, ruff - do they pass?</step>
  <step order="4" name="PATTERNS">Were existing patterns followed? Check similar code.</step>
  <step order="5" name="TESTS">Are tests meaningful? Cover edge cases and errors?</step>
  <step order="6" name="SECURITY">Any OWASP vulnerabilities? Input validation?</step>
  <step order="7" name="COMPLEXITY">Is this the simplest possible solution?</step>
  <step order="8" name="COMPLETENESS">Is the original plan fully implemented? Are docs/, architecture/ (read-only), README.md, PLAN.md consistent with the actual implementation? Any stubs or missing features?</step>
  <step order="9" name="PROMPT-QUALITY">Any new prompt files in planwerk/prompts/? Check each for clear purpose, no redundancy, measurable value, proper XML structure, and integration into builder/constants/agent code.</step>
</thinking>

<mindset>
  Question EVERYTHING - assume over-engineered until proven otherwise.
  If bloated or messy: recommend rewrite, not patch. Preserve functionality but demand clean, minimal implementation.
  Don't accept "it works" as justification for bad code.
</mindset>

  <!-- BLOCKING: Must pass, otherwise verdict = BLOCKED -->
  <section name="automated-verification" severity="blocking">

    <check id="C4">Errors raised explicitly (not None or silent failures)</check>
    <check id="C5">No regression in existing functionality</check>

  BLOCKED: Any blocking check fails → fix blocking issues first, re-request review

<quality-principles enforce="strict">
  ELEGANT: Reject bloated implementations | DRY: Reuse existing utilities | KISS: Simplest solution |
  YAGNI: No unused code, no future-proofing | SOLID: Single responsibility | NO_COMPAT: No backward compat hacks unless required |

<anti-patterns>
